title: What training does the EU Carcinogens, Mutagens and Reprotoxic Substances Directive require?
description: What Article 11 of Directive 2004/37/EC requires for training on carcinogens, mutagens and reprotoxic substances, including healthcare and the 2026 amendment.
shortAnswer: Directive 2004/37/EC on carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances at work requires employers to give workers sufficient and appropriate training on health risks, exposure precautions, hygiene, protective equipment, and incident response. Since Directive (EU) 2022/431, Article 11 also requires the training to be adapted to new or changed risks, provided periodically in healthcare settings, including for hazardous medicinal products, and repeated periodically in other settings if necessary. Exposure lists and medical records must be kept for 40 years.
keyTakeaways: Article 11(1) lists five training topics: health risks including the added risk from tobacco, precautions, hygiene, protective equipment, and incident steps for workers and rescue workers.
Directive (EU) 2022/431 extended the directive to reprotoxic substances and made periodic training mandatory in healthcare settings; Member States had to transpose it by April 5, 2024.
Exposure lists and medical records must be kept for at least 40 years after exposure ends for carcinogens and mutagens, and at least five years for reprotoxic substances.
Directive (EU) 2026/2450, published on October 30, 2026, adds welding fumes, tightens PPE rules, and must be transposed by November 20, 2028.
The European Commission published guidance on hazardous medicinal products in 2023 and an indicative list in 2025, both useful inputs to healthcare training.
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National labor inspectorates enforce the transposing laws; the European Commission monitors transposition; the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) publishes guidance
appliesTo: Employers whose workers are or are likely to be exposed to carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances
Healthcare workers who prepare, administer, or dispose of hazardous medicinal products
Rescue and maintenance workers who may face abnormal or planned higher exposure
Welders and other workers exposed to process generated CMR substances

sections.heading: What is Directive 2004/37/EC and who does it cover?

blocks.text: [Directive 2004/37/EC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02004L0037-20240408) of April 29, 2004 is the European Union law protecting workers from risks related to exposure to carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances (CMR substances) at work. It is the sixth individual directive under the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), and Article 1(3) confirms the Framework Directive applies fully, without prejudice to the stricter provisions in this directive.

Article 3(1) applies the directive to activities in which workers "are or are likely to be exposed" to CMR substances as a result of their work. A carcinogen, mutagen, or reprotoxic substance is defined in Article 2 primarily as a substance or mixture meeting the criteria for category 1A or 1B under the Classification, Labelling and Packaging (CLP) Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, plus substances, mixtures and processes listed in Annex I of the directive. Article 1(2) excludes workers exposed only to radiation covered by the Euratom Treaty, which is addressed on [the EU radiation protection training page](/regulations/eu-radiation-protection-basic-safety-standards-training).

According to [EU-OSHA's summary of the directive](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directives/directive-2004-37-ec-carcinogens-or-mutagens-at-work), five amendments were adopted between 2017 and 2024 (Directives 2017/2398, 2019/130, 2019/983, 2022/431 and 2024/869), and Directive 2022/431 brought reprotoxic substances into scope, changing the directive's title.

sections.heading: What does Article 11 require for training?

blocks.text: Article 11(1) requires the employer to take appropriate measures so that workers and/or their representatives "receive sufficient and appropriate training, on the basis of all available information, in particular in the form of information and instructions". The training must cover five topics:

items: potential risks to health, including the additional risks due to tobacco consumption
precautions to be taken to prevent exposure
wearing and use of protective equipment and clothing
steps to be taken by workers, including rescue workers, in the case of incidents and to prevent incidents

blocks.text: As substituted by Directive 2022/431, Article 11(1) then sets three rules on timing. Training must be adapted to new or changed risk, "in particular when workers are or are likely to be exposed to new carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances or to a number of different" CMR substances, including those in hazardous medicinal products, or when work circumstances change. It must be "provided periodically in healthcare settings" to all workers exposed to CMR substances, in particular where new hazardous medicinal products are used. In other settings it must be "repeated periodically" if necessary.

Article 11(2) adds information and labeling duties. Employers must inform workers of installations and containers holding CMR substances, label them clearly and legibly, and display warning and hazard signs. Where a biological limit value is set in Annex IIIa, health surveillance is mandatory and workers must be informed of that requirement before being assigned to the task.

sections.heading: What does the directive mean for healthcare training?

blocks.text: Healthcare is the one setting where the directive makes periodic training an explicit, unconditional requirement for exposed workers. Hazardous medicinal products that contain one or more CMR substances fall within the directive's scope, so pharmacists, nurses, and support staff who prepare, administer, or dispose of them are covered.

Article 18a of the consolidated directive required the Commission to prepare Union guidelines on the preparation, administration and disposal of hazardous medicinal products and, where appropriate, to establish a definition and an indicative list. EU-OSHA reports that the Commission published a guidance document in 2023, which "also serves as a useful reference point and support for training activities", and a Communication with the definition and an indicative list in 2025.

A healthcare training program should map each product on its formulary that appears on that list to the roles that handle it, so that the arrival of a new product triggers the periodic training Article 11 now requires. The broader healthcare context is covered on the [healthcare and life sciences industry page](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

sections.heading: Which obligations apply to which roles, and what evidence is expected?

blocks.text: Training duties attach to exposure, so the role map starts from the list of exposed workers that Article 12(c) requires the employer to keep. The table shows each obligation, who it applies to, its frequency, and the evidence an inspector would expect.

blocks.text: The retention periods in Article 15 are far longer than most learning systems keep data by default. Training records that prove what an exposed worker was taught are often requested alongside exposure records in occupational disease claims, so it is prudent to align their retention with the exposure list. The trade offs are covered in [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How do hygiene and protective equipment rules shape the training content?

blocks.text: Training topics (c) and (d) mirror the hygiene and protection duties in Articles 5 and 10, so the content should teach workers to apply the specific controls the employer has put in place. Article 10(1) requires that workers do not eat, drink or smoke where there is a risk of contamination, that protective and street clothing are stored separately, and that protective equipment is checked and cleaned if possible before, and in any case after, each use. Article 10(2) states that workers may not be charged for these measures.

Article 5 sets a strict hierarchy: exposure must be prevented, a closed system used where replacement is not technically possible, and otherwise exposure reduced to as low a level as is technically possible for carcinogens, mutagens and non-threshold reprotoxic substances. Training on personal protective equipment therefore teaches the last line of defense, and it is most credible when it explains why the higher controls are in place.

[Directive (EU) 2026/2450](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32026L2450) of October 21, 2026 was published in the Official Journal on October 30, 2026. It enters into force on the twentieth day after publication, and Member States must transpose it by November 20, 2028. As at November 2026 it is adopted but not yet applicable through national law.

items: **Welding fumes:** Annex I gains a new point 9 covering work involving exposure to fumes from welding processes containing substances or mixtures classified as category 1A or 1B carcinogens, mutagens or reproductive toxicants.

**Personal protective equipment:** a new subparagraph in Article 5(5) states that PPE, in particular respiratory protective devices, is a last resort and must be correctly chosen, individually adjusted to fit the wearer, and maintained under Directive 89/656/EEC.
**Breaks:** a new Article 10(3) entitles workers wearing PPE to regular breaks in an area without contamination risk, with duration and frequency set by the risk assessment.
**Limit values:** Annex III revises the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons entry, and the replaced Annex IIIa sets biological limit values for lead and for 1,4-dioxane.

blocks.text: For training owners, the individual fit requirement for respiratory protection and the welding fume entry are the changes most likely to require new content. Planning now, using the method in [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change), avoids a rush when national laws arrive.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each CMR substance, its controls, and the five Article 11 topics as linked concepts with assessment points, tied to the exposed roles. When a new hazardous medicinal product or a revised limit value is added, the affected concepts and people are identifiable from those links, and the version history supports the long retention periods the directive sets.

faqs.q: Does Directive 2004/37/EC set a fixed retraining interval?
faqs.a: No number is set. In healthcare settings training must be provided periodically to all exposed workers; elsewhere it must be repeated periodically if necessary and adapted when risks change. The employer, or the national transposing law, sets the actual interval, and the rationale should be documented.

faqs.q: Why does the training have to mention tobacco?
faqs.a: Article 11(1)(a) expressly requires training on potential risks to health, "including the additional risks due to tobacco consumption". Smoking can compound the harm from some carcinogens, and Article 10(1)(a) separately prohibits smoking in working areas where there is a risk of contamination.

faqs.q: Are reprotoxic substances treated the same as carcinogens?
faqs.a: Mostly, with differences. Since Directive 2022/431, Article 11 training covers reprotoxic substances in the same way. Threshold reprotoxic substances must be reduced to a minimum rather than to the lowest technically possible level, and records are kept for five years rather than 40.

faqs.q: How does this directive relate to the Chemical Agents Directive?
faqs.a: The Chemical Agents Directive is the general rule for hazardous chemicals; Directive 2004/37/EC adds stricter, specific requirements for CMR substances. Where both apply, employers follow the stricter provision. See [the EU Chemical Agents Directive training page](/regulations/eu-chemical-agents-directive-worker-training).
